note: What each task in tasks_v1.json was chosen FOR. Deliberately a separate file: the counting side gets the task lines with no comment column and counts, per task, how many of the lint's four rules a natural solution would trigger. Only afterwards does it see this. A blind check that can read the answer key is not one.
why_this_exists: The first draft of the list was to be written by the side that also wrote the lint, with the rule 'name a program, never a construct'. That rule is necessary and not sufficient — the bias sits in WHICH programs get picked, not in how they are worded. 'Print a triangle of stars' names no construct and forces the loop the C99 trap lives in. Named by the parallel session, 2026-08-06.
the_condition_that_makes_the_experiment_: The list MUST contain traps the lint does NOT know. Otherwise the decisive comparison measures a tool against itself and 'with lint is better' is a tautology rather than a finding.
lint_knows: a declaration in the for initialiser

lint_does_not_know.char_signedness: The classic one, and K&R warns about it itself: `char c; while ((c = getchar()) != EOF)` cannot work where char is unsigned, and the loop either never ends or ends early. Invited by every task that reads characters until end of input.
lint_does_not_know.missing_prototype: C89 wants a function declared before it is called. A program that puts main first and its helpers after gets an implicit declaration — which SC diagnoses and no regex here catches.
lint_does_not_know.old_style_parameters: K&R-era sources declare parameters between the parenthesis and the brace. A model imitating the source material may reproduce it. Legal C89, but it interacts badly with prototypes elsewhere in the same file.
lint_does_not_know.integer_width: Assumptions about how wide an int is, which do not survive the move to a 68k compiler — most visible in the bit tasks and in anything that shifts by more than fifteen places.
lint_does_not_know.declaration_after_statement: A genuine C89 rule the lint deliberately does not check, because finding it reliably needs a parser and a wrong flag is worse than a missing one. Invited by any task long enough to have a second block.

expected_by_task.t02, t03, t04, t05, t06, t07, t26, t40: char signedness — these read characters until end of input
expected_by_task.t08, t09, t35, t39: arrays plus a helper function: missing prototype, and the widest surface for a declaration after a statement
expected_by_task.t16..t25: string handling without the library — prototypes, and the pointer-versus-array habits K&R teaches
expected_by_task.t27..t31: integer width and shift counts on a 68k compiler
expected_by_task.t32, t33, t34: loops with two indices — the densest ground for the for-head rule the lint DOES know
expected_by_task.t36, t37, t38, t39: arrays of structures and static tables — old-style declarations most likely here
expected_by_task.t01, t10..t15: plain loops and formatted output, chosen as the low-trap baseline the distribution needs

one_word_kept_on_purpose: Three tasks say 'array' (t32, t33, t34). A check for construct-naming flags it, and it stays: 'array' names the DATA, not a piece of syntax, and it steers towards none of the four rules the lint knows. Calling it something else would have made the task ambiguous rather than neutral — and an ambiguous task measures the wording. Recorded here so the decision is visible rather than merely made.
honest_uncertainty: This is what the tasks were chosen for, not what they will produce. If the counting side's blind distribution comes out skewed against this table, that is a finding about the list — and it is available BEFORE the measurement rather than after it, which is the only reason for doing it this way.
